Dev Uthani vrat katha
Once upon a time, there lived a king with enormous wealth. During Ekadashi, he restrained himself from eating anything and never let anyone from his kingdom eat. Once, a servant of the king refused to keep a fast, so the king gave him flour, rice and lentils and asked him to go to the riverbank and cook the food himself. He cooked food and, with full devotion, prayed to Lord Vishnu to come and eat. The deity came, ate the food and went to his abode.
On the next Ekadashi, the servant asked for double the rations, saying that he had run out of food the previous time. The king was astonished and decided to secretly observe. When the Lord did not immediately arrive after the food was prepared on the riverbank, the servant threatened to jump into the river and commit suicide. Lord Vishnu appeared, stopped him, ate the food and finally took him to Vaikuntha on his vahan. The king understood that devotion done with a pure heart and love, rather than mere formality or show, leads to the attainment of God.

Devutthana Ekadashi is one of the most significant Ekadashis dedicated to Lord Vishnu. The word “Devutthana” can be understood as the awakening or rising of the divine. According to Hindu tradition, Lord Vishnu enters a state of Yoga Nidra, or yogic sleep, on Devshayani Ekadashi and awakens approximately four lunar months later on Devutthana Ekadashi.
This period is known as Chaturmas or Chaturmasya. It is traditionally regarded as a time of restraint, devotion, introspection, fasting and spiritual practice. Puranic traditions describe Lord Vishnu as resting on Sheshanaga in the cosmic Kshira Sagara during this period.
But does Lord Vishnu literally sleep like a human being?
The deeper meaning of the tradition goes far beyond physical sleep. Vishnu’s Yoga Nidra represents a cosmic state of withdrawal, stillness and inwardness. His awakening on Devutthana Ekadashi symbolically represents renewed activity, awareness, auspicious beginnings and movement from inner preparation into conscious action.
That is why the significance of Lord Vishnu waking up has both a religious and a profound spiritual dimension.
What Is Devutthana Ekadashi?
Devutthana Ekadashi falls on the Ekadashi Tithi of Kartik Shukla Paksha, the waxing phase of the lunar month of Kartik. It is also called Dev Uthani Ekadashi, Prabodhini Ekadashi, Devotthani Ekadashi and Hari Bodhini Ekadashi in different traditions.
The word “Prabodhini” itself relates to awakening or becoming conscious.
In 2026, Devutthana Ekadashi is commonly listed for Friday, November 20, 2026, while certain Vaishnava observances fall on November 21. The Kartik Shukla Ekadashi Tithi runs across this period, and exact fasting observances can differ according to tradition and location.
Devotees traditionally worship Lord Vishnu, observe an Ekadashi vrat, chant his names, offer Tulsi leaves and engage in prayer and devotional practices.

Why Does Lord Vishnu Sleep for Four Months?
According to traditional Hindu belief, Lord Vishnu enters Yoga Nidra on Devshayani Ekadashi, which occurs during Ashadha Shukla Paksha.
This marks the beginning of Chaturmas.
Lord Vishnu is described as resting upon Sheshanaga in Kshira Sagara, the cosmic ocean, until his awakening on Devutthana or Prabodhini Ekadashi. The period from Ashadha Shukla Ekadashi to Kartik Shukla Ekadashi is therefore traditionally associated with Vishnu’s yogic rest.
However, Yoga Nidra should not simply be understood as ordinary sleep.
In yogic and spiritual symbolism, sleep or withdrawal can represent turning consciousness away from constant external activity. Chaturmas similarly encourages devotees to reduce distractions, practise discipline and focus more deeply on spiritual development.
Therefore, the four months are not merely about the deity “sleeping.” They are also an invitation for the individual to pause and look within.
